ptfe.origin: PTFE fiber is made from polytetrafluoroethylene, a fluoropolymer polymerized from tetrafluoroethylene gas through industrial fluorine chemistry. Fluoropolymer manufacture historically used perfluorinated surfactants such as PFOA as polymerization aids, which later drew regulatory attention to the whole supply chain. Fibrous PTFE products are niche: split-film and monofilament yarns, staple for needle-punched filter felts, sewing threads for filter bags, expanded PTFE membranes and hollow fibers. Many products described as 'PTFE fabric' are laminates of an expanded PTFE membrane on another textile rather than PTFE fiber.
ptfe.structure: PTFE's chain is a carbon backbone fully sheathed in fluorine atoms, which twist it into a helix. The strong carbon-fluorine bonds and the fluorine sheath give very low surface energy, low friction, chemical inertness and hydrophobicity. Molar masses reach several million grams per mole, so melt viscosity is far too high for conventional melt spinning. When PTFE paste is extruded and stretched, it develops a microstructure of nodes interconnected by fine fibrils, the basis of expanded PTFE membranes and hollow fibers; dense PTFE lacks these fibrils.
ptfe.process: Because it cannot be melt spun, PTFE fiber is made by indirect routes. In paste extrusion, fine PTFE powder is mixed with a lubricant, extruded, dried, stretched and heated; stretching develops the node-and-fibril structure, and the stretching ratio controls pore size and porosity, with higher ratios raising porosity at the expense of strength. Split-film fiber is made by slitting and fibrillating stretched films, and PTFE split fibers are carded and needle-punched, sometimes with PPS fibers, into filter felts. PTFE hollow-fiber membranes are made by paste extrusion, stretching and heating in the same way.
ptfe.performance: PTFE withstands almost all chemicals, including strong acids and oxidants, and tolerates high service temperatures, which suits hot corrosive gas filtration and chemical-plant packing. Its low surface energy helps dust cakes release during pulse-jet cleaning, and hydrophobic PTFE hollow fibers kept high filtration efficiency after washing. Weaknesses are low tensile strength, creep and cold flow under load, high density and cost, and poor dyeability. Heated to decomposition, PTFE releases fumes that cause polymer fume fever, a flu-like illness that can progress to lung injury; one reported case involved a plastics machinist who smoked after handling micronized PTFE.
ptfe.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should not be attempted: PTFE does not ignite readily, and its decomposition fumes are hazardous. Practical clues are high density, a waxy slippery feel and resistance to almost all solvents. FTIR shows strong carbon-fluorine absorptions, and thermal analysis shows a high crystalline melting transition. Scanning electron microscopy distinguishes expanded PTFE, with nodes linked by fibrils, from dense PTFE or from split fibers with rough, grooved surfaces.
ptfe.labeling: Fiber content must use the applicable generic name from 16 CFR 303.7 in the US and a fibre name from Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 in the EU; Teflon is a trademark. A garment with a PTFE membrane is labeled by the fibers of its fabric layers. PTFE counts as a PFAS under broad chemical definitions: reviews authored by fluoropolymer producers argue it meets 'polymer of low concern' criteria, while EU restriction proposals have debated covering fluoropolymers as a class.
ptfe.past: PTFE entered textiles through industrial rather than apparel needs: filter bags, threads, packings and membranes for environments too hot or corrosive for other polymers. Expanded PTFE made the polymer porous and breathable, opening filtration, medical and outerwear uses. Its recent history is shaped by PFAS regulation. Studies authored or funded by fluoropolymer producers report that PTFE did not degrade or release non-polymeric PFAS in environmental fate tests and that incineration under best available technology produced no significant amounts of the PFAS studied; an independent review notes that complete breakdown of PTFE requires incineration from about 850 C.

pps.origin: PPS fiber is spun from poly(p-phenylene sulfide), an engineering thermoplastic made, in the generally described route, by polycondensation of p-dichlorobenzene with sodium sulfide in a polar solvent. The same resin is molded into automotive and electrical parts, and only part of it becomes fiber. The main textile market is needle-punched filter felt and bags for baghouses that clean hot flue gas from power plants, municipal waste incinerators and industrial boilers, where the felt is a consumable replaced on a schedule.
pps.structure: The PPS chain alternates para-linked benzene rings with sulfur atoms in thioether links. The rigid, symmetrical chain crystallizes readily, giving a semicrystalline fiber with a high melting point, low moisture uptake and resistance to acids, alkalis and most solvents. The thioether sulfur is also its weak point: strong oxidants oxidize it to sulfoxide and sulfone groups and can cross-link the chains, and in hot, oxidizing flue gas this shortens service life. Researchers have turned this into a treatment, oxidizing PPS fibers with hypochlorous acid into sulfone-rich fibers with better high-temperature and oxidation resistance.
pps.process: PPS resin is dried and melt spun: the polymer is extruded through spinnerets, quenched, drawn and heat set to develop crystallinity, then crimped and cut to staple. For filtration, staple is carded into webs, layered onto a woven scrim and needle-punched into felt, which is heat set and finished, sometimes with a PTFE treatment. Research adds functional layers to such felts, including sprayed reduced graphene oxide, cross-linked polybenzoxazine coatings, layer-by-layer PTFE and silica coatings, and manganese-cerium-cobalt oxide catalysts that destroy dioxins and nitrogen oxides while filtering dust.
pps.performance: PPS is inherently flame resistant and hydrolysis resistant, and it keeps its properties in hot, acidic, moist flue gas where polyester would hydrolyze. Its limits are oxidative attack in gases rich in oxygen or nitrogen oxides at elevated temperatures, which shortens bag life, and a finite continuous service temperature. It is stiff and not used for apparel. Pulse-jet cleaning performance can be improved: in one test, a plain PPS filter medium released about 62 percent of its dust cake at a blowback speed of 0.3 m/s, and a graphene oxide coated version about 75 percent.
pps.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: PPS is difficult to ignite, chars and self-extinguishes, with a sulfurous smell. FTIR shows aromatic and carbon-sulfur bands and, after oxidative aging, sulfoxide and sulfone bands, which helps diagnose degraded filter bags. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and elemental analysis detect sulfur, separating PPS from aramid, polyimide or PTFE felts. In used bags, dust and coatings must be removed before analysis.
pps.labeling: PPS is sold mainly as industrial filter media rather than consumer textiles, but when fiber content is stated on regulated textile products, US labels use a generic name from 16 CFR 303.7 and EU labels a fibre name from Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. In procurement, the relevant documents are the felt's technical data sheet, filtration efficiency and pressure-drop test results and the plant's emission permit, not the fiber name alone.
pps.past: PPS fiber grew from engineering-polymer development and from the need for felts that could survive hot, acidic, humid combustion gas in pulse-jet baghouses at power plants and waste incinerators. Current research aims to extend its service life and add functions: coatings that protect against oxidation, catalytic PPS filters that in one study destroyed 78 percent of dioxins and furans and converted 96 percent of nitric oxide at 200 C, triboelectric PTFE and PPS felts that charge themselves during carding and needling, and fluorescent filter bags intended for condition monitoring.
